title: Xi Jinping’s Grandiose Timidity
text:
T he APEC summit , hosted this week by Chinese President Xi Jinping and attended by Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, among dozens of other leaders and luminaries, provided China with a chance to show its diplomatic heft. Never before had the leaders of the three biggest nuclear powers gathered to discuss the affairs of the world, or their plans to harness its potential or divide it up among themselves. If Xi wanted to use his enormous influence for some constructive purpose, this would have been a good time to try.

 Nearly 1,000 journalists signed up to see the spectacle at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, some of them (like myself) flying halfway around the world to watch history emerge from all of the powerful people packed into one place. But when all the public speeches had been made in Shenzhen and all the private talks adjourned, the sum of it amounted to nothing historic, which seemed to be the host’s intention. Xi avoided any public debate about the world’s most pressing crises. He confined the summit’s agenda to vague statements about innovation and cooperation, and he left the visiting journalists to sift in vain through his pronouncements for nuggets of news that might match the event’s potential.

 At least the White House kept our expectations low. In a pre-summit call with reporters, a senior U.S. official lamented that China did not want to talk about nuclear-arms control. “We do think it’s time for China to step up to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said. “They can’t just take their ball and go home.”

 Xi seemed to disagree. He made sure the summit looked important without needing to decide important things. He posed for a photo with all of his illustrious guests while keeping their discussions away from the cameras. It’s possible that behind closed doors, the summit resulted in deals that its participants have chosen to keep to themselves. We wouldn’t know, because Xi made sure the world could see only a sanitized version of great-power diplomacy. China watchers often attribute his fondness for the uneventful to various features of the national character: strategic patience, risk aversion, the wisdom of the tortoise over the reckless Western hare. But Xi’s refusal to do the messy work of ending wars looked a lot more timid than cunning this week.

 A lot of Xi’s power over world events derives from China’s economic dynamism, and he could not have chosen a better place than Shenzhen to put it on display. Two generations ago, the city was hardly more than a cluster of fishing villages across the bay from Hong Kong. Today, Shenzhen has a population of roughly 18 million people (more than 10 times that of Manhattan), and it serves as a hub of China’s tech industry and an engine of its AI revolution.

 By the time I arrived on Monday, the city had switched into summit mode. Banners on many streets proclaimed the themes of the gathering: Openness Innovation Cooperation . A more honest slogan might have included the word Control. Miles of police barricades surrounded parks and lined boulevards, preventing people from walking anywhere near the APEC venue. My hotel had an APEC information desk in the lobby, but the friendly young people behind it were unable or unwilling to tell me where the APEC summit would be held. They could share only the address of the APEC Media Center, located several miles away from the summit itself.

 Throughout the day, buses to the media center pulled up every few minutes at a gargantuan convention hall, which may go down in history as the most elaborate holding pen ever devised for the press. Inside, an army of minders provided us with every comfort—a limitless buffet of Chinese food, humanoid-robot baristas, massage chairs, and sleeping masks—but no access to the APEC summit or any of its noteworthy participants.

 Hundreds of reporters roamed around this space or sat scrolling on their phones. The more enterprising among them, determined to generate content, asked other reporters for interviews and filmed their opinions about the summit. Screens suspended above the media center showed footage from an APEC side event known as the CEO Summit. But there was no sound, and the QR code for the audio track led me to an error page that never finished loading.

 As my taxi slowed down near the entrance to the summit in Shenzhen, the self-styled “City of the Future,” Chinese policemen came running. Although I could not understand them, their shouting made me brace for a night in jail or the shock of a stun gun. Thankfully, my press credentials calmed the officers enough to let me approach their security checkpoint. But that’s as far as they let me go.

 Finally, on Wednesday afternoon, Trump gave headline writers something to work with. Descending the stairs of Air Force One, the U.S. president leaned in for a bro hug with Xi, who had come to greet his guest on the tarmac at the Shenzhen airport. By the placid standards of the summit, this qualified as breaking news, at least insofar as it placed Xi in a situation that he did not appear to have choreographed. From my place in the viewing stand, about a hundred yards away, it was impossible to hear what the two men briefly whispered to each other.

 [ Read: The deferential president ] 

 T he next day , when Xi and Trump sat down with Putin for their first trilateral meeting, the Chinese leader opened with a statement about the Second World War and the need to avoid a third one in the future. But he did not bring up the two wars that his guests are currently fighting in Europe and the Middle East. Instead, he called for the United States, Russia, and China to create a nuclear-crisis hotline or, as he described it, “prevention mechanisms to ensure that misjudgments are minimized.” The gesture showed a hint of openness from Xi to engage on nuclear issues with the Americans, though it fell far short of the disarmament talks that Trump and his predecessors have long sought with China.

 Earlier in the day, Xi’s speech to the summit stuck closely to the generic topics his government had plastered around town. The leaders gathered in Shenzhen must “expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi told the summit’s opening banquet, according to the official translation. Make what you will of this verbiage, but it did not exude an eagerness on China’s part to roll up its sleeves and fix the planet’s problems.

 Wealth and status, of course, do not necessitate any particular willingness to act. No one expects the sultan of Brunei, another guest at APEC this week, to resolve conflicts or reduce the likelihood of Armageddon. But the leader of a superpower, whether ascendant or established, does bear some responsibility for engaging in matters of war and peace, and Xi showed little interest in carrying that burden this week.

 Maybe that is for the best. Few would want China to project its power the way Russia has done in recent years, through brutality against its neighbor and thuggery just about everywhere else. But Putin does not portray himself as a benevolent force in the world. He has been candid about his desire to tear apart the Western order and rebuild it to his liking.

 Xi cultivates a different image. He tries to be seen, in contrast to Putin and Trump, as a force for stability, a convener of nations and steward of the status quo. To his credit, he has reportedly talked Putin down from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. But that does not make him a peacemaker. Nearly five years into the war, Xi has done little to stop it. He has continued selling the technology that Ukraine and Russia use to manufacture weapons, apparently content to let their conflict weaken Europe and transform Moscow into an economic vassal of Beijing.

 [ Read: NATO’s nightmare ] 

 Nor has Xi spent much political capital on ending the war in Iran, whose regime has relied on trade with China to rebuild its arsenal and continue fighting. In his rhetoric and public actions, Xi has done his best to keep a distance from these wars, pretending that they are none of China’s business. He has abstained from all organized efforts to mediate peace, perhaps because these efforts continue falling flat. In fairness to Xi, most leaders would rather not associate themselves with intractable conflicts and diplomatic failures. But he can’t really have it both ways.

 He can’t host the presidents of the two nuclear superpowers, both of whom are waging wars against far smaller nations, without offering any public thoughts about those wars or the possible paths to their conclusion. He can’t invite his chief rivals in the race to create intelligent machines and then elide the topic of this race and the threats it poses to humanity. Failing to contend in any outward way with these era-defining problems suggests that Xi does not aim to exercise power. He aims to hoard it and put it on display.
